title: Exponents and radicals
competency: Use exponents, roots and the laws of exponents, simplify radicals, and apply the properties of real numbers.

keywords.def: In aⁿ, the exponent n says how many times the base a is multiplied by itself. Also called the power.
In aⁿ, the number a that is multiplied.
If a² = b, then a is a square root of b.
If a³ = b, then a is a cube root of b.
If aⁿ = b, then a is an nth root of b.
The real nth root ⁿ√b: positive when b > 0, negative when b < 0 and n is odd, 0 when b = 0.
The small number n in ⁿ√b. No index means square root.
The number under the radical sign: b in ⁿ√b.
Radicals with the same index and the same radicand, such as 2√5 and 7√5. Only like radicals can be added.
A set is closed under an operation if doing it to two members always gives a member of the set.
The number −a that gives 0 when added to a. Also called the opposite.
The number 1/a that gives 1 when multiplied by a (a ≠ 0). Also called the reciprocal.

en.text: aⁿ means a multiplied by itself n times. a is the base and n is the exponent. For a ≠ 0, a⁰ = 1 and a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ. To multiply powers of the same base, add the exponents. To divide, subtract them.

am.text: aⁿ ማለት a ራሱን n ጊዜ ሲባዛ ነው። a መሠረት፣ n አርቢ ነው። a ≠ 0 ሲሆን a⁰ = 1 እና a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ ነው። ተመሳሳይ መሠረት ያላቸውን ስታባዛ አርቢዎቹን ደምር፤ ስታካፍል ቀንስ።

screens.text: 2⁴ = 16, 2³ = 8, 2² = 4, 2¹ = 2. Each time the power drops by 1, the value is halved.
screens.ask: Keep the pattern going. What is 2⁰?
screens.after:
Halve 2 and you get 1, so 2⁰ = 1.
"0" is tempting, but halving never reaches 0.
Halve again: 2⁻¹ = 1/2, 2⁻² = 1/4. Read on.

screens.title: Exponents
paras: Writing 14 × 14 × … × 14 twenty times takes time and space. Exponents make this short.
Definition 1.9: If a is a real number and n is a positive integer, then a × a × … × a (n times) = aⁿ.
Here a is the base and n is the exponent (power).
Notice that (−3)⁴ and −3⁴ are different. The brackets decide what is raised to the power.

screens.title: Base and exponent
defs: In aⁿ, the number a that is multiplied by itself.
In aⁿ, the number n that says how many times a is used. Also called the power.

screens.title: Spot the base
screens.text: Look at 7⁵.
screens.ask: Base and exponent: which number is the base of 7⁵?
screens.why:
7⁵ = 7 × 7 × 7 × 7 × 7.
The base is the number being multiplied: 7.
The exponent 5 says how many 7s.
35 and 75 only join the digits: they are not parts of 7⁵.
screens.clue: The base is the big number; the exponent sits up high.

screens.title: Zero and negative exponents
paras: Activity 1.16: moving right lowers the power by 1, so divide by 2 each time.
So 2⁻ⁿ = 1/2ⁿ. In the same way, a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ for a ≠ 0.
Note 1. Zero exponent: if a ≠ 0, then a⁰ = 1.
Note 2. Negative exponent: if a ≠ 0 and n is a positive integer, then a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.

screens.title: Halve each time
screens.text: Move right: the power drops by 1, so divide by 2.

screens.title: A negative exponent
screens.text: Negative exponent: what is 5⁻²?
screens.why:
Rule: a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.
5⁻² = 1/5².
5² = 25, so 5⁻² = 1/25.
−25 is wrong: a negative exponent gives a reciprocal, not a negative number.

screens.title: Mind the brackets
screens.text: Mind the brackets: what is −3⁴?
screens.why:
Without brackets, only 3 is raised to the power 4.
3⁴ = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81.
Then put the minus in front: −81.
81 would be (−3)⁴, with brackets.

screens.title: Laws of exponents
paras: Activity 1.17 compares pairs such as 2³ × 3³ and (2 × 3)³. Each pair is equal.
The pairs give these laws, for a, b real and m, n natural numbers.
Tap each law below to see an example.

screens.title: Laws of exponents
screens.ask: Tap each law to see an example.

screens.text: Simplify both sides of each pair and compare.

screens.title: Add the exponents
screens.text: Use aⁿ × aᵐ = aⁿ⁺ᵐ.
screens.ask: Multiply powers with the same base: 3⁴ × 3² = 3 to the power ___
screens.why:
Same base 3, so add the exponents.
4 + 2 = 6.
So 3⁴ × 3² = 3⁶.
Check: 81 × 9 = 729 = 3⁶.
screens.clue: Do you add or multiply the exponents when you multiply powers?

screens.title: A school message
screens.text: A message starts with one student in a school in Hawassa. Each round, every student who has it sends it to 2 new students. After 5 rounds, 2⁵ new students get it in the last round.
screens.why:
2⁵ means five 2s multiplied.
2 × 2 = 4, then 4 × 2 = 8.
8 × 2 = 16, then 16 × 2 = 32.
So 32 students get it in round 5.

en.text: If aⁿ = b, then a is an nth root of b. The principal nth root ⁿ√b is the real one we use. Even roots of negative numbers are not real. b^(1/n) means ⁿ√b. Only like radicals, with the same index and radicand, can be added.

am.text: aⁿ = b ከሆነ a የ b n-ኛ ሥር ነው። ዋናው n-ኛ ሥር ⁿ√b የምንጠቀምበት እውን ሥር ነው። የአሉታዊ ቁጥር ጥንድ ሥር እውን አይደለም። b^(1/n) ማለት ⁿ√b ነው። ተመሳሳይ ሥሮች ብቻ ይደመራሉ።

screens.title: A square courtyard
screens.text: A square church courtyard in Lalibela has an area of 81 m².
screens.ask: How long is each side? Take a guess.
screens.after:
9 × 9 = 81, so each side is 9 m.
40.5 is 81 ÷ 2: that halves the area, it does not undo squaring.
Finding the side undoes squaring. That is taking a root. Read on.

screens.title: Find the side
screens.note: Move the slider until the area is 81 m². The side is then √81 = 9 m.

screens.title: Roots
paras: Definitions 1.10 and 1.11: If a² = b, a is a square root of b. If a³ = b, a is a cube root of b.
If aⁿ = b, a is an nth root of b.
For n > 1, the principal nth root ⁿ√b is the positive nth root if b > 0.
It is the negative nth root if b < 0 and n is odd. It is 0 if b = 0.

screens.title: Kinds of roots
defs: If a² = b, then a is a square root of b.
If a³ = b, then a is a cube root of b.
If aⁿ = b, then a is an nth root of b.
ⁿ√b: positive if b > 0; negative if b < 0 and n is odd; 0 if b = 0.

screens.title: Real or not?
screens.text: Real roots: which root is NOT a real number?
screens.why:
√(−9): no real number squared gives −9, because 3² = 9 and (−3)² = 9.
Odd roots of negatives are real: ∛(−8) = −2 and ⁵√(−32) = −2.
√0 = 0 is real.
So √(−9) is not a real number.
screens.clue: Is the index even or odd?

screens.title: Radical sign, index and radicand
paras: In ⁿ√b, √ is the radical sign, n is the index and b is the radicand.
With no index written, √ means square root.
Definition 1.12: If n is a positive integer greater than 1, then b^(1/n) = ⁿ√b, whenever ⁿ√b is a real number.
screens.note: Correction: the printed Definition 1.12 says 'if b ∈ ℝ' with no condition. When n is even, b must not be negative: (−4)^(1/2) is not a real number.

screens.title: Parts of a radical
defs: The small number n in ⁿ√b. No index means square root.
The number under the radical sign: b in ⁿ√b.

screens.title: Examples 1 and 2
screens.text: Finding roots, and writing roots as powers.

screens.title: Laws for rational powers
paras: The laws of exponents also work for powers 1/n and for rational powers a^(m/n) = (a^(1/n))^m.
screens.note: Correction: in Example 4(b) the printed text says 'Both numbers 32 and 64 are multiples of 2', but the numbers in the question are 32 and 162.

screens.title: A rational power
screens.text: Rational power: simplify 4^(3/2).
screens.clue: Take the square root first, then cube.

screens.title: Adding and subtracting radicals
paras: Activity 1.18: √2 − √2 = 0 and 4√2 − √2 = 3√2 are correct.
Definition 1.13: Radicals with the same index and the same radicand are like radicals. 2√5, −(2/3)√5 and √5 are like radicals. √2 and √3 are not; √3 and ∛3 are not.

screens.title: Like radicals
defs: Radicals with the same index and the same radicand, such as 2√5 and √5.

screens.text: Add or subtract like radicals as you collect like terms. Sometimes simplify first.

screens.title: Find the cube inside 54
screens.intro: Tap ▶. Look for three equal primes.
say: 54 = 2 × 27. 2 is prime, so it is a leaf.

screens.title: Collect like radicals
screens.why:
√8 = √(4 × 2) = 2√2.
Now 2√2 + √2 = (2 + 1)√2.
So √8 + √2 = 3√2.
√10 is wrong: roots do not add under one sign.
screens.clue: First write √8 as a number times √2.

screens.title: A field in Bishoftu
screens.text: A square field in Bishoftu has an area of 50 m². Its side is √50 m.
screens.ask: Simplify the root: which is √50 in simplest form?
screens.why:
Find the largest perfect square in 50: 25.
50 = 25 × 2.
√50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2.
The side is 5√2 m ≈ 7.07 m.
screens.clue: Find the largest perfect square that divides 50.
screens.worked: 50 = 25 × 2, and 25 is a perfect square. √50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2. So the side is 5√2 m ≈ 7.07 m.

ideas.name: Operations and properties of real numbers

en.text: ℝ is closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by non-zero numbers. A rational plus an irrational is irrational. Every real number a has an additive inverse −a. Every non-zero a has a multiplicative inverse 1/a. Zero has no reciprocal.

am.text: ℝ በመደመር፣ በመቀነስ፣ በማባዛትና ዜሮ ባልሆነ ቁጥር በማካፈል ዝግ ነው። ምክንያታዊ ሲደመር ኢ-ምክንያታዊ ኢ-ምክንያታዊ ይሆናል። እያንዳንዱ a የመደመር ተቃራኒ −a አለው። ዜሮ ያልሆነ a የማባዛት ተገላቢጦሽ 1/a አለው።

screens.text: Rational or irrational? Make your best guess for each result.
items: Adding 2 does not stop π's decimal.

screens.title: Operations on real numbers
paras: The rational numbers obey the commutative, associative and distributive laws.
Adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing (except by 0) two rational numbers always gives a rational number. ℚ is closed under these operations.
The irrational numbers obey the same laws. But the sum, difference, product or quotient of two irrationals is not always irrational.
Activity 1.19: √3 × √12 = 6 is rational. A rational and an irrational can never have a rational sum or difference. 2 ÷ √2 = √2 is irrational.

screens.title: Closed sets
defs: A set is closed under an operation if the result is always in the set. ℚ is closed under +, −, × and ÷ (not by 0).

screens.title: Find the irrational one
screens.text: Rational or irrational: which result is irrational?
screens.why:
(1 − √3)(1 + √3) = 1 − 3 = −2: rational.
√8 × √2 = √16 = 4: rational.
√12 ÷ √3 = √4 = 2: rational.
3 + √5: rational + irrational is irrational.

screens.title: Conclusions
paras: The sum or difference of a rational number and an irrational number is irrational.
The product or quotient of a non-zero rational number and an irrational number is irrational.
Because ℝ contains all the rational and irrational numbers, ℝ is closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication and division (except division by 0).

screens.title: Two irrationals
screens.text: Product of two irrationals: what is √3 × √12?
screens.why:
√3 × √12 = √(3 × 12) = √36.
√36 = 6.
So two irrationals gave a rational product.
√15 is a slip: it adds 3 + 12.

screens.title: Properties of addition and multiplication
paras: Activity 1.20 asks for opposites and reciprocals. The opposite of √3 is −√3. The reciprocal of 3^(2/3) is 3^(−2/3).
These are the inverse properties. Tap each property below.

screens.title: Properties of addition and multiplication
items: a + b and ab are real numbers.
a + b = b + a and ab = ba.
(a + b) + c = a + (b + c) and (ab)c = a(bc).
a + 0 = 0 + a = a and a × 1 = 1 × a = a.
a + (−a) = 0: −a is the additive inverse. a × (1/a) = 1 for a ≠ 0: 1/a is the reciprocal.
a(b + c) = ab + ac and (b + c)a = ba + ca.

screens.title: Inverses
defs: −a, because a + (−a) = 0. Also called the opposite.
1/a for a ≠ 0, because a × (1/a) = 1. Also called the reciprocal.

screens.text: Additive and multiplicative inverses.

screens.title: No reciprocal
screens.text: Multiplicative inverse: which real number has no multiplicative inverse?
screens.why:
The inverse of a is the number that makes a × (inverse) = 1.
0 × anything = 0, never 1.
So 0 has no multiplicative inverse.
1, −1 and √2 have inverses 1, −1 and 1/√2.

screens.title: Find the reciprocal
screens.ask: Find the reciprocal: the multiplicative inverse of 0.25 is ___.
screens.why:
Write 0.25 as a fraction: 0.25 = 1/4.
Flip it: the reciprocal of 1/4 is 4.
Check: 0.25 × 4 = 1.

screens.title: Shopping in Gondar
screens.text: Abel buys 3 notebooks at 12 birr and 3 pens at 8 birr in Gondar. He works out 3 × (12 + 8) = 60 birr instead of 3 × 12 + 3 × 8.
screens.ask: Which property of real numbers lets him do this?
screens.why:
He writes 3 × 12 + 3 × 8 as 3 × (12 + 8).
That is a(b + c) = ab + ac with a = 3, b = 12, c = 8.
This is the distributive property.
Both ways give 60 birr.
screens.clue: Look at the table row where × spreads over +.
screens.worked: 3 × 12 + 3 × 8 = 36 + 24 = 60. 3 × (12 + 8) = 3 × 20 = 60. This is a(b + c) = ab + ac, the distributive property.

items.ask: Write the root as a power: √5 = ___
items.why:
A square root has index 2.
b^(1/n) = ⁿ√b, so √5 = 5^(1/2).
Check: 5^(1/2) × 5^(1/2) = 5¹ = 5.
items.clue: A square root is the power 1/2.

items.ask: Write the root as a power: ∛(3⁴) = ___
items.why:
A cube root is the power 1/3.
∛(3⁴) = (3⁴)^(1/3).
Multiply the exponents: 4 × 1/3 = 4/3.
So ∛(3⁴) = 3^(4/3).
items.clue: A cube root is the power 1/3; then multiply exponents.

items.why:
(−27)^(1/3) means ∛(−27).
Which number cubed gives −27?
(−3) × (−3) × (−3) = 9 × (−3) = −27.
So the answer is −3.
items.clue: Which number cubed gives −27?
Which number to the 5th power is 32?
Find each root separately.
Which decimal squared gives 0.09?

items.why:
Largest perfect square in 125: 25.
125 = 25 × 5.
√125 = √25 × √5 = 5√5.
items.clue: Find a perfect square that divides 125.

items.why:
Same power 1/3, so divide inside: (9/243)^(1/3).
243 = 9 × 27, so 9/243 = 1/27.
∛(1/27) = 1/3, because 3³ = 27.
So the answer is 1/3.
items.clue: Use aⁿ/bⁿ = (a/b)ⁿ first.

items.ask: Fifth root of a decimal: ⁵√0.00032 = ___
items.clue: 2⁵ = 32. Count the decimal places.

items.ask: Add exponents with the same base: 2^(3/2) × √2 = ___
items.why:
√2 = 2^(1/2).
Same base, so add exponents: 3/2 + 1/2 = 4/2 = 2.
2² = 4.
items.clue: Write √2 as a power of 2, then add exponents.

items.ask: Find each root, then add: ∛0.001 + ⁴√0.0081 = ___
items.clue: Find each root, then add.

items.why:
Same power 1/4, so multiply inside: (3 × 27)^(1/4).
3 × 27 = 81.
81^(1/4) = 3, because 3⁴ = 81.
items.clue: Use (a × b)ⁿ = aⁿ × bⁿ backwards.
Simplify √12 first.
Find a perfect cube that divides 54.
Each root is a whole number.

items.text: Add radical expressions: x = 4√2 + 7√5 and y = √2 − 3√5. Find x + y.
items.why:
Collect the √2 terms: 4√2 + √2 = 5√2.
Collect the √5 terms: 7√5 − 3√5 = 4√5.
So x + y = 5√2 + 4√5.
9√7 is wrong: √2 and √5 are not like radicals.
items.clue: Collect the √2 terms and the √5 terms.

items.text: Subtract radical expressions: x = 4√2 + 7√5 and y = √2 − 3√5. Find x − y.
items.clue: Subtracting −3√5 adds 3√5.

items.why:
Multiply the numbers: 2 × 4 = 8.
Multiply the roots: √5 × √3 = √15.
So 2√5 × 4√3 = 8√15.
items.clue: Multiply the numbers, then the roots.

items.why:
Divide the numbers: 4 ÷ 2 = 2.
Divide the roots: √6 ÷ √2 = √3.
So 4√6 ÷ 2√2 = 2√3.
items.clue: Divide the numbers, then the roots.
Simplify √18 first.

items.text: Inverses: find the additive and multiplicative inverse of −2/5.
items.why:
Additive inverse: change the sign: 2/5. Check: −2/5 + 2/5 = 0.
Multiplicative inverse: flip the fraction and keep the sign: −5/2.
Check: (−2/5) × (−5/2) = 10/10 = 1.
items.clue: The reciprocal keeps the same sign.

items.text: Inverses: find the additive and multiplicative inverse of 0.111… (0.1 repeating).
items.why:
0.111… = 1/9.
Additive inverse: −1/9.
Multiplicative inverse: flip 1/9 to get 9.
Check: 1/9 × 9 = 1.
items.clue: Change the repeating decimal to a fraction first.

items.text: Name the property of real numbers: √3(√3 − 2) = 3 − 2√3.
items.why:
√3 multiplies each term in the bracket.
√3 × √3 = 3 and √3 × 2 = 2√3.
That is a(b − c) = ab − ac: the distributive property.
items.clue: Which property spreads × over a bracket?

items.text: Name the property of real numbers: 5 + (−8 + 2) = (5 − 8) + 2.
items.why:
The numbers stay in the same order: 5, −8, 2.
Only the brackets move.
Changing the grouping is the associative property.
Both sides equal −1.
items.clue: What moved: the order or the brackets?

items.text: True or false? Every real number has a multiplicative inverse.
items.why:
0 × anything = 0, never 1.
So 0 has no reciprocal.
Every other real number a has 1/a.
So the statement is false.
items.clue: Try to find the reciprocal of 0.

items.text: True or false? The operation a ∗ b = 2a + b is commutative.
items.why:
Commutative means a ∗ b = b ∗ a every time.
1 ∗ 2 = 2 × 1 + 2 = 4.
2 ∗ 1 = 2 × 2 + 1 = 5.
4 ≠ 5, so it is not commutative: false.
items.clue: Try a = 1 and b = 2 both ways.

test.why:
a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.
2⁻³ = 1/2³.
2³ = 8, so 2⁻³ = 1/8.
−8 is wrong: a negative exponent is not a negative number.

test.text: True or false? The sum of a rational number and an irrational number is always irrational.
test.why:
Suppose r + x = q, with r and q rational and x irrational.
Then x = q − r, which would be rational.
That is impossible, so the sum is irrational.
True. Example: 3 + √5.

notes.text: Definition 1.12: the printed text says 'if b ∈ ℝ' with no condition. When n is even, b must not be negative: (−4)^(1/2) is not a real number. The unit summary (item 11) adds the right condition.
Example 4(b): the printed text says 'Both numbers 32 and 64 are multiples of 2', but the numbers in the question are 32 and 162.

Exercise 1.29 item 4(b), √145 − √232 + √261, does not simplify to a single radical: 145 = 5 × 29, 232 = 4 × 58 and 261 = 9 × 29. The answer is √145 − 2√58 + 3√29. The numbers may be a printing error. Teacher review needed. The item is left out of the exercise set here.

Exercises are capped at six items each. Left out: 1.26 1(b), 1(d), 1(e); 1.27 (e), (g), (h), (j); 1.29 2(c), 3(c), 4(a), 4(b); 1.30 1(a), 1(c), 2(c), 4(b). Activity 1.20 is summarised in a read block.

Order: in the book the laws of exponents (Activity 1.17 and the table) come after roots (Definitions 1.10–1.12). Here the laws table sits in the exponents idea, and the rational-power examples (Examples 3 and 4) stay in the roots idea.

Powers like b^(1/n) are written with ^ because the lesson text is plain; the book uses superscripts. Added examples: Hawassa message, Lalibela courtyard, Bishoftu field, Gondar shopping, √8 + √2, 3⁴ × 3², 7⁵ and 0.25 items.

screens.title: Sign rules
screens.text: Count the negative signs when you multiply.

screens.title: Your turn
screens.text: What is (−2)³?
screens.why:
(−2) × (−2) = 4.
4 × (−2) = −8.
Three negatives give a negative.
−6 is a slip: it multiplies −2 × 3.
screens.clue: An odd number of negatives gives a negative.

screens.title: Undo a square
screens.text: A square root undoes squaring.

screens.title: Your turn
screens.text: What is √12 in simplest form?
screens.why:
12 = 4 × 3, and 4 is a perfect square.
√12 = √4 × √3 = 2√3.
3√2 is √18, not √12.
screens.clue: Find the largest perfect square that divides 12.

screens.title: Rational or irrational?
screens.text: Look at the decimal form of the number.
steps: A rational number can be written a/b, with integers a, b and b ≠ 0.
Its decimal ends, like 0.75, or repeats, like 0.111… = 1/9.
An irrational decimal neither ends nor repeats.

screens.title: Your turn
screens.text: Which number is irrational?
screens.why:
0.25 and 2/3 are fractions: rational.
√9 = 3: rational.
5 is not a perfect square: √5 = 2.23606… never ends or repeats.
So √5 is irrational.
screens.clue: Is the number under the root a perfect square?
